correctness.rationale: For each pair of iid uniform spherical sites, the coarea formula applied to the bisector F(z)=z·(Xi-Xj)=0 has the exact gradient |Xi-Xj| on its zero set. Conditional on equal uniform site heights c, the chance that all n-2 other sites lie below c is ((1+c)/2)^(n-2). Relative azimuth contributes sin(Delta/2); after spherical area, height and azimuth density normalizations, the expected pair-interface measure has density sqrt(1-c²) sin(Delta/2) ((1+c)/2)^(n-2) dc dDelta. The transformations U=(1+c)/2 and Z=cos(Delta/2) give independent Beta(n-1/2,3/2) and uniform[-1,1], hence V=1-Z² is Beta(1,1/2). Its integral yields 16B(n-1/2,3/2) per pair, the exact binomial formula for expected total length, all Q moments and the Exp(1) limit by beta-gamma multiplication. Algebraic rational moment checks and independent geometric simulation from the embedded checker passed. A zero-arclength triple-tie set is treated correctly; the n=2 full great-circle boundary is included.

originality.rationale: The precise new contribution is the finite-binomial, annealed arclength-weighted joint law for the common site-height and generator chord factor, together with exact total interface length, all chord moments and their exponential scaling limit. The inspected primary theorems on binomial spherical Voronoi face counts do not imply metric-length formulas; spherical Poisson large-cell deviations are for another model and observable. The earlier accessible three-site area distribution and great-circle tessellation moments concern different statistics. Closest classical 1971 source is inaccessible and remains a specific historical priority risk rather than grounds for fabricated certification.

value.rationale: The problem is a standard natural finite-binomial spherical Voronoi model, but face counts alone leave metric interface behavior unknown. The theorem gives the complete arclength-weighted joint two-generator metric mark law, each chord moment at any n, an exact expected total interface length, a nontrivial curvature correction to its planar scaling and an exponential distance limit. These facts form a structurally informative finite-size benchmark, not arbitrary numerical recomputation or an elementary restatement of the face-vector theorems.
